children: Scott Bessent has his reward for an August of financial engineering: a bond market selloff. On Tuesday, as he gathered the G20’s finance ministers and central bankers in Asheville, North Carolina, long-end bond yields in the U.S., Japan, Germany, and elsewhere shot up. The freakout owes to a dog’s breakfast of concerns including runaway deficits, Iran and trade war inflation pressures, and the credibility of fiscal and monetary authorities in the U.S. To stop the bleeding, the Trump administration will need more than a rehash of old ideas such as overly rosy promises of tariff revenue, fraud prevention, and growth.

Bessent has dusted off his hedge-fund manager hat this summer. First he dipped into foreign-exchange reserves to stabilize the yen. Then he doubled the U.S. Treasury's buybacks to stem a rout in long-term government bonds. His efforts have had limited success: the yen remains weak, and 30-year Treasury yields are hovering around 5.2%.

Rather than trading distortions in markets, however, the Treasury should be heeding their signals. Right now, they are warning about the fiscal and geopolitical situation. The United States’ $2.1 trillion 2026 budget deficit threatens to worsen next year, as Trump’s tax policy drains revenue and the defense budget balloons — possibly to $1.5 trillion, as requested — to absorb the costs of the Iran war.

Investors don't seem to foresee a default, or the U.S. printing money to avoid one. Inflation-adjusted bond yields imply an annual increase of 2.3% on average over the next 10 years, in line with historical records. But the inability to bring deficits down does threaten to overheat the economy at some point.

Bessent has promised a deficit reduction plan. Yet it will essentially continue what the White House is already doing: increased tariff revenue, combating fraud in social welfare programs and, of course, growth. This doesn't pass the smell test. If renewed trade levies even survive legal challenges, duties of up to 12.5% slapped on 60 countries will only barely lower the projected path of national debt, the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget reckons.
Meanwhile, total fraud and improper payments in social benefit programs probably doesn't add up to much more than $200 billion, according to government estimates.

Help will thus have to come from elsewhere. It won’t be Congress, at least not in the near term: deficit reduction is not on the table before the November midterms. So only the Federal Reserve is left. Though Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh has no say over budgets, he can cool the economy by further tightening financial conditions. Markets are now expecting a September rate hike. It won’t erase the August mess, but it’s a start.
Follow Gabriel Rubin on Bluesky and LinkedIn.
Global bond yields traded at multiyear highs on September 1 as finance leaders from the Group of 20 gathered in Asheville, North Carolina for a ministerial meeting.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a CNBC interview on August 21 that there's a "very good chance" the federal deficit has peaked and that "several hundred billion dollars" could be saved by cutting waste, fraud and abuse from government spending.

The United States on July 24 imposed new tariffs of 10% and 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners, including the EU and China, alleging those countries failed to curb imports made by forced labor, just as a temporary 10% global tariff expired.
